# dsh-session-mail
Send a message from the agent in one DSH session to the agent in another session of the same host.
The delivery is one-way. To answer, the receiving agent calls the same tool once more, addressing th
e sender by the session id that arrived in the message header.
## What the receiver sees

The first line carries the sender's session id, so the receiving agent knows the message came from a
nother agent (not from the human) and knows where to answer. The receiving side needs no extra machi
nery: the message arrives as an ordinary prompt in the target session, and the tool description tell
s the model what the `From` header means.
## The third tool: `create_session`
Creates a conversation and returns its id, in-process through `sessionController.create`:
| argument | meaning |

| `cwd` | directory the session runs in; omit for the host default |
| `agentPreset` | optional pres

directory the session runs in; omit for the host default |
| `agentPreset` | optional preset name |
It exists because the Web route is no longer usable for this: `POST /api/session/create` needs a v2
operator credential that only the per-process launch token can mint.
## The tool
`send_session_message`
| argument | type | meaning |
| `toSessionId` | string | Target session id (`session-<32 hex>`). When answering, use the id from t

he `From` header. |
| `message` | string | The text to say. The plugin prepends the `From` header. |
| `urgent` | boolean | `false` (default) — send in order: the message waits for the target's curren
t turn to end. `true` — interject: the message is injected into the target's running turn right away
urn to end. `true` — interject: the message is injected into the target's running turn right away. |
## The other tool: `read_session_info`
Reading another session is read-only: it does not resume the target and delivers nothing to it.
`read_session_info`
| argument | type | meaning |

| `sessionId` | string | Target session id. |
| `what` | `title` \| `last_reply` \| `last_present` \
| `status` \| `all` | Which field to fetch; `all` is the default (`status` is fetch-only, so `all` l
ll` | Which field to fetch; `all` is the default (`status` is fetch-only, so `all` leaves it out). |

- `title` — the session title, from `session/projections`.
- `last_reply` — the final assistant mess
age of the last completed turn (`turnOutline`, last non-empty `response`). A turn that is still runn

ing has an empty response, so it is skipped.
- `last_present` — the last `present` tool call of the
session: the files it declared as deliverables with their descriptions, found by paging back through
`session/page` (the cold-safe history route) and reading the raw `tool/call` events.
Both routes answer for a cold session: `session/projections` returned the title of a session whose a
gent was not running, and `session/page` returned its events.
### Message ids, threads and recalls
Every message carries a `[mail m-xxxxxxxx …]` line under the `From` header. That id is what the othe
r side quotes in `replyTo`, and what you pass in `supersedes`.
| argument | effect |

| `replyTo` | marks the message as an answer; the id shows up in the metadata line |
| `thread` | a
task name. While a message with the same thread is still pending for that session, a second one retu

rns `skipped` with `dedupe: "pending-thread"` and the earlier id in `prior` |
| `supersedes` | ids o
f earlier messages that are no longer valid. Still-pending ones are removed before this message is q
ueued (`superseded`); already-delivered ones come back in `notRecalled` |
Only still-pending messages can be recalled: the host has no way to rewrite a message that already l
anded. The plugin remembers the bodies it sent in this process, so a restart forgets them and `notRe
called` is the honest answer.
`read_session_info(sessionId, "status")` answers "is the peer busy, and what is queued": `busy` (the
last event of the session is not `turn/end`), `queuedNextTurn` / `queuedNextStep`, `lastEvent`, `la
stInbound` (the most recent mail it received, with its id) and `lastOutbound` (the most recent mail
this process sent to it).
## Queue or interject: `urgent`
`urgent` picks how the message is handed to the target session:
| `urgent` | host mode | inbox target | when it lands |
| `false` (default) | `queue` | `next-turn` | after the target's current turn ends — it becomes the

first step of the next turn |
| `true` | `steer` | `next-step` | at the next step of the target's *c

the next turn |
| `true` | `steer` | `next-step` | at the next step of the target's *current* turn |
Measured 2026-10-29 against a live peer session, four cases:
| peer state | inbox target | landing |
| busy, one long turn | `next-turn` (queue) | 21 s later, first step of the *following* turn — after

the whole running turn |
| idle | `next-step` (steer) | a new turn started immediately |
| running
a 90 s foreground command | `next-step` (steer) | after that command returned — still inside the sam

e turn |
| running a background job plus 5-second steps | `next-step` (steer) | **4.0 s** later, in
the next step of the *same* turn, while the background job still had ~49 s to run |
The rule behind those numbers: **a steer takes effect at the next step boundary, and the delay is ro
ughly the remaining time of the tool call the current step is executing.** It never waits for the tu
rn to end, but it cannot preempt a tool call that is already running — a foreground command blocks t
he step, while a background job does not block the turn at all.
The host also downgrades a steer to a queue in one case: if the agent's current turn was already abo
rted, the message goes to `next-turn` instead (`send()` resolves the target to `next-turn` when the
abort signal is set).
**When to pick which** — a correction has to travel on the interrupting channel:
- **`urgent: true`** — a message that *invalidates something the recipient already received*: a corr
ection, a retraction, a changed conclusion. Queued, it would land only after the recipient has finis

hed acting on the wrong instruction and burned the tokens for it.
